segments.voice: Yesterday, a teaching role in the house: Upakosala's teacher was away, and the fires he tended taught him. Today, a father at home who gets asked something he can't answer.
screen: `THE FIRES TAUGHT HIM.` · `TODAY: A QUESTION WITH NO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: A kid asks a question at bedtime, and the grown-up's mind goes blank. There's a quick way out: say something confident and change the subject. The Chandogya Upanishad has that moment, with higher stakes. A young man, Shvetaketu, comes home stung. At a king's assembly he was asked questions about where people go when they leave this world, and he couldn't answer one. You told me you'd taught me everything, he says to his father. What does his father say?
screen: `A BEDTIME QUESTION.` → `A SON COMES HOME STUNG.` → `YOU SAID YOU'D TAUGHT ME.`

segments.voice: His father, Gautama, doesn't defend himself. You know me, he says. Whatever I knew, I told you. I don't know even one of these. Then he does something harder. He goes to the king himself. At the palace the king offers him worldly wealth. Gautama turns it down: keep that; tell me what you said to my son. The king is uneasy, asks him to stay a while, and then teaches him. A father sits down to learn from a king. So a teaching role in the house, in this story, includes a plain sentence: I don't know either. And it includes walking out the door to find out. That closes the summit's two weeks. A lake and a yaksha's question. A hymn that asks who really knows. A graduate's send-off, a bath, a bow. A chain back to Brahma, a list of names, a boy who told the truth, a teaching lost and told again. Then the house: three teachers at one table, fires that taught, and a father who said I don't know. Lineage and house turn out to be one thread. The line goes on because someone in a house keeps asking.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW EVEN ONE.` · `KEEP THE WEALTH; TEACH ME.` · `A FATHER LEARNS FROM A KING.` · `ONE THREAD: KEEP ASKING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring up one question you can't answer yet, about your life, a text, or someone you love. Hold it lightly with the breath and let it stay unanswered. If you pray, you can offer the question just as it is; if not, let it sit beside you like a guest.
A teaching role in the house: in the Chandogya, a father admits he doesn't know, and goes out to learn.

howItsDone: In some Hindu families, questions about God, death and the rites go from child to parent to grandparent, and sometimes on to a priest or teacher; saying 'let's find out' is part of how the tradition is handed down at home.

original.note: Sanskrit: Shvetaketu, the son who comes home stung; his father is Gautama (Uddalaka Aruni).

Chandogya 5.3 was taught in year two (day 338) for the five fires; this day takes the father's admission and his going to learn. The king's questions are left uncounted (the text gives five). The draft's line 'this knowledge had not gone to brahmins before' (5.3.7) was cut for length; the script says only that the king, uneasy, teaches him.

Whether Gautama formally approaches as a pupil here is clearer in the Brihadaranyaka parallel (6.2); the script says only that he sits down to learn. The original note names him Uddalaka Aruni; confirm.
